questions.text:
Which one of the options given below refers to the degree (or arity) of a relation in
relational database systems?
questions.solution:
Degree (arity) = number of attributes (columns) in the relation schema.
The number of tuples (rows) is called the cardinality.

Answer: Number of attributes of its relation schema

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Number of attributes of its relation schema.
Number of tuples stored in the relation.
Number of entries in the relation.
Number of distinct domains of its relation schema.

questions.text:
Suppose two hosts are connected by a point-to-point link and they are configured
to use Stop-and-Wait protocol for reliable data transfer. Identify in which one of
the following scenarios, the utilization of the link is the lowest.
questions.solution:
Stop-and-wait utilization [latex]=\frac{T_t}{T_t+2T_p}=\frac{1}{1+2a}[/latex], where [latex]a=\frac{T_p}{T_t}[/latex].

Utilization is lowest when [latex]a[/latex] is largest:
- longer link [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] larger [latex]T_p[/latex]
- higher transmission rate [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] smaller [latex]T_t[/latex]

Answer: Longer link length and higher transmission rate

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Longer link length and lower transmission rate
Longer link length and higher transmission rate
Shorter link length and lower transmission rate
Shorter link length and higher transmission rate

questions.text:
Let [latex] A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 &4 \\ 4& 1& 2 &3 \\ 3& 4 & 1 &2 \\ 2 &3 &4 &1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex] B=\begin{bmatrix} 3& 4 & 1 &2 \\ 4& 1& 2 &3 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 &4 \\ 2 &3 &4 &1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Let det(A) and det(B) denote the determinants of the matrices A and B, respectively.
Which one of the options given below is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Rows of B are rows of A in the order [latex]R_3,R_2,R_1,R_4[/latex], i.e. B is A with rows 1 and 3 swapped.

One row swap changes the sign of the determinant: [latex]\det(B)=-\det(A)[/latex].

Answer: det(B) = [latex]-[/latex]det(A)

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: det(A) = det(B)
det(B) = - det(A)
det(A)=0
det(AB) = det(A) + det(B)

questions.text:
Consider the following definition of a lexical token [latex]id[/latex] for an identifier in a programming language, using extended regular expressions:

[latex] letter \rightarrow [A-Za-z][/latex]
[latex] digit \rightarrow [0-9][/latex]
[latex] id \rightarrow letter (letter\;| \;digit)^*[/latex]


Which one of the following Non-deterministic Finite-state Automata with - transitions accepts the set of valid identifiers? (A double-circle denotes a final state)
questions.solution:
An identifier is one letter followed by any mix of letters and digits.

- (A): the [latex]\epsilon[/latex] edge lets the string skip the first letter, e.g. "1" or the empty string is accepted [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- (B): after choosing a branch you stay with only letters or only digits; "a1b" is rejected [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- (C): letter, then from the final state any number of letter-or-digit steps through the loop [latex]\text{---}[/latex] correct.
- (D): forces "letter digit" pairs; "ab" is rejected [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.

Answer: C

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: A
B
C
D

questions.text:
An algorithm has to store several keys generated by an adversary in a hash table. The adversary is malicious who tries to maximize the number of collisions. Let [latex] k[/latex] be the number of keys, [latex] m[/latex] be the number of slots in the hash table, and [latex] k \gt m[/latex].
Which one of the following is the best hashing strategy to counteract the adversary?
questions.solution:
Any fixed hash function (division or multiplication) is known to the adversary, who can pick keys that all collide.

Universal hashing picks the hash function at random from a family at run time, so the adversary cannot predict it, and the expected number of collisions stays small.

Answer: Universal hashing method

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Division method, i.e., use the hash function [latex]h(k) = k\;  mod \; m[/latex]

Multiplication method, i.e., use the hash function [latex] h(k) =  \left \lfloor m(kA -\left \lfloor kA \right \rfloor ) \right \rfloor[/latex], where
[latex]A[/latex] is a carefully chosen constant.
Universal hashing method.
If [latex]k[/latex] is a prime number, use Division method. Otherwise, use Multiplication method
